title: Notice the little things
tagline: Seven small observations, on seven different days.
story: A year begins quietly. Before doing anything ambitious, we start by looking: the light on a wall, a stranger's kindness, the sound a kettle makes. Noticing is a skill, and like most skills it gets easier with a little practice.
why: Writing down one thing you noticed is a simple way to practise paying attention. It asks nothing of you except a moment.
instructions: On any day this month, write down one thing you noticed that you might normally walk past.
One observation counts per day. Seven different days completes the month.
Entries are private and stay yours. A sentence is plenty.
prompts: What did you notice today that you'd usually miss?
What was the light like today?
What small sound stood out?
What did someone do today that was quietly kind?
What looked different from yesterday?
What did you enjoy for a few seconds today?
What detail would you put in a painting of today?
reflectionPrompt: Which observation surprised you most when you read it back?
completionLine: January is officially one for the books.

title: Give your brain a workout
story: Nine rows, nine columns, nine squares, and one rule. Sudoku needs no arithmetic and no general knowledge, only patience and a willingness to rule things out. February is short; five puzzles fit it nicely.
why: A little exercise for the part of your mind that likes figuring things out. Sudoku is practice in logical reasoning, working through constraints, and staying with a problem.
instructions: Each row, column and 3×3 square must contain the numbers 1–9 exactly once.
Solve five different puzzles this month. Your place is saved automatically, so stop whenever you like.
Pencil marks and hints are there to be used. A hinted puzzle still counts.
reflectionPrompt: Was there a moment a puzzle suddenly opened up? What changed?
completionLine: February is officially one for the books.

title: Build your core
tagline: Thirty minutes of planking, added up across the month.
story: Not thirty minutes at once — thirty minutes in total, in whatever pieces suit you. Twenty seconds here, a minute there. By the end of March those small holds add up to something you can feel.
why: Short, regular holds are a simple way to practise core strength and body awareness. The month rewards showing up, not straining.
instructions: Start the timer, hold a plank for as long as feels steady, then pause or finish.
Rest as often as you like. Only time on the clock counts; paused time never does.
Reach 30 minutes in total before the month ends.
safetyNote: Keep a straight line from shoulders to heels and breathe normally. Stop if you feel pain, dizziness or discomfort; rest is part of the practice. If you have an injury or a health condition, check with a professional first.

accessibleAlternative.title: Seated core hold
accessibleAlternative.detail: Sit tall near the front of a chair, feet flat, and gently draw your stomach in while you breathe steadily. Lean back a few degrees if comfortable. It counts minute for minute, exactly like a plank.

reflectionPrompt: How did the first session compare with the last?
completionLine: March is officially one for the books.

title: Find beauty in the ordinary
tagline: Ten photos of everyday details most people overlook.
story: A door handle worn smooth. Shadows of a fence. Fruit in a bowl. April asks you to look at ordinary things as if they had been placed there on purpose, and to keep ten of them.
why: Looking for something worth photographing changes how a familiar place feels. It's practice in seeing.
instructions: Take or choose a photo of an everyday detail you find quietly beautiful.
Add a caption if you'd like to remember why.
Collect ten this month. Photos stay on your iPhone.
reflectionPrompt: Which of the ten would you hang on a wall?
completionLine: April is officially one for the books.

title: Read a little further
tagline: Read and log sixty pages of a book.
story: Sixty pages is a few evenings, or two pages a day. It can be a novel you abandoned, a book someone gave you, or something you have always meant to start. May is for getting a little further in.
why: Reading a book asks for a different kind of attention than a screen does. Sixty pages is enough to remember what that feels like.
instructions: Tell us what you're reading. More than one book is fine.
Log the pages you read whenever you put the book down.
Sixty pages in total completes the month.
reflectionPrompt: What's one line or idea from your reading that stayed with you?
completionLine: May is officially one for the books.

title: Learn another language
tagline: Learn twelve words and show you can recall them.
story: Twelve words will not make you fluent. They will let you greet someone, thank them, and ask for bread — which is how every language begins. Pick one and make a small start.
why: Learning a handful of words in another language is a friendly way to practise memory, and a small courtesy to the people who speak it.
instructions: Choose a language and study its twelve words with the flashcards.
Listen to each word, then practise until they feel familiar.
Pass the recall exercise — at least 10 of 12 — to complete the month. You can retake it as often as you like.
reflectionPrompt: Which word are you most likely to actually use?
completionLine: June is officially one for the books.

title: Do something good
story: Hold a door. Send the message you've been meaning to send. Let someone go first. July is for five small, deliberate kindnesses — and for noticing how they felt.
why: Kindness is easy to intend and easy to forget. Writing it down afterwards makes it a little more likely to happen again.
instructions: Do something kind for someone — small is fine.
Afterwards, write a line about what you did. It stays private.
Five entries complete the month.
prompts: What did you do, and for whom?
What small thing made someone's day easier?
Who did you check in on?
What did you give — time, attention, help?
reflectionPrompt: Which of these would you like to make a habit?
completionLine: July is officially one for the books.

title: Make something new
tagline: Prepare three dishes you've never made before.
story: It doesn't have to be elaborate. A salad dressing from scratch, a flatbread, a soup from whatever's in season. August is for three small firsts in the kitchen.
why: Making something you haven't made before is a low-stakes way to practise following your curiosity — and you get to eat the result.
instructions: Choose something you've never prepared. Simple recipes count.
Make it, then log its name. Add a photo or a note if you like.
Three new dishes complete the month.
prompts: What did you make?
What was new about it for you?
How did it turn out?

accessibleAlternative.title: No-cook or assisted recipes
accessibleAlternative.detail: Assembling counts as much as cooking: a new sandwich, a fruit plate, a cold drink, or a dish made together with someone else.

reflectionPrompt: Which dish would you make again, and what would you change?
completionLine: August is officially one for the books.

title: Get moving
tagline: One hundred and twenty minutes of intentional walking.
story: Two hours across a whole month: a few loops of the block, a longer route home, a walk with a friend. The only rule is that you set out on purpose.
why: Walking on purpose, without it being the way to somewhere else, encourages intentional movement and a little time with your own thoughts.
instructions: Start the timer when you set out and finish it when you're done.
Walks can be any length. They add up across the month.
Reach 120 minutes in total. No location is ever recorded.
safetyNote: Go at a pace that lets you talk comfortably, and stop if anything hurts.

accessibleAlternative.title: Any intentional movement
accessibleAlternative.detail: Wheeling, gentle stretching, chair exercises, swimming or any movement you choose on purpose counts minute for minute.

reflectionPrompt: Where did your favourite walk take you?
completionLine: September is officially one for the books.

title: Make something from nothing
tagline: Take one creative project through three stages.
story: A poem, a sketch, a song, a shelf, a short film on your phone. October gives you three steps: choose an idea, make a rough first version, then improve or finish it. Finished beats perfect.
why: Most ideas stall before the first rough version. Three small stages are a gentle way to practise getting past that.
instructions: Stage one: write down the idea you've chosen.
Stage two: make a first version and record it with a note or a photo.
Stage three: improve or finish it, and record what changed.
reflectionPrompt: What did the second version teach you that the first didn't?
completionLine: October is officially one for the books.

title: Take back your attention
tagline: Ten focused sessions of ten minutes each.
story: Ten minutes, one thing, nothing else. Read, write, think, practise, tidy a drawer — anything you choose to give your full attention. Do it ten times this month.
why: Ten uninterrupted minutes is short enough to start and long enough to notice the pull of distraction. It's practice in sustained attention.
instructions: Decide what you'll focus on, then start the ten-minute timer.
Put your phone face down. A sound and a notification mark the end.
A session counts when the full ten minutes are complete. Ten sessions complete the month.
reflectionPrompt: What did you do with your best ten minutes?
completionLine: November is officially one for the books.

title: Remember your year
story: The year is nearly a memory. Before it becomes one, choose twelve moments worth keeping — large or small — and write a line about each. Then look back at everything you collected.
why: Looking back on purpose turns a blur of months into a handful of stories you can actually tell.
instructions: Think back over 2027 and write down a moment that mattered.
Add a photo if you have one. Everything stays private unless you choose to share.
Twelve moments complete the month and unlock your Year in Review.
prompts: A moment from this year you want to remember…
A day that went better than expected…
Someone who made this year better…
Something you did for the first time…
A place you were glad to be…
Something small that made you laugh…
reflectionPrompt: If you could keep only one of these twelve, which would it be?
completionLine: December is officially one for the books.
